title: Front Brake Pad and Rotor Replacement

parts.name: Inner / outer wheel bearings + races (if repacking)

citations.title: Dana 44 / Dana 44HD TTB Front Axles (Blue Oval Trucks)

summary: Front rotors on the Dana 44 TTB Bronco are 11.72" diameter with a 0.96" discard thickness. The 1987–1992 trucks use tension-pin calipers and the 1994–1996 trucks use two-bolt calipers — buy the right caliper hardware kit for your year. Pad/rotor jobs on this truck always include a wheel-bearing repack, because the rotor and the bearings come off as one assembly.
description:
This is brake work, and brake work is safety-critical. Take the warning labels seriously: brake dust contains material you don't want in your lungs, brake fluid attacks paint, and a caliper bolt that's not torqued correctly will let go on the highway. If anything during this job feels wrong, stop and double-check torque values and bleed condition.

The Dana 44 TTB hub is the key complication. On most modern vehicles, the rotor sits in front of the hub and pulls off independently. On the 1980–1996 Bronco, the rotor is sandwiched between the inner and outer wheel bearings — meaning to pull a rotor, you also pull the hub. That means you're touching the wheel bearings every time you do front brakes, and you should treat every pad-and-rotor service as a bearing-repack service. Buying new bearings is cheap insurance; the L68149/L68111 (outer) and LM67048/LM67010 (inner) bearing-and-race sets are well under $60 for both sides.

Calipers come off easily once you support them. Don't let a caliper dangle from the soft brake hose — hang it from the spring with a bungee or coat hanger. If the slide pins are seized (they almost always are on a 30-year-old truck), replace the slide pin kit. Seized slides cause uneven pad wear and pulsing brakes that look like warped rotors.

Bearing preload is set by feel after torque. Tighten the inner spindle nut to 50 ft-lb while rotating the rotor back and forth — this seats the bearings. Back the inner nut off about 45 degrees so the rotor turns freely with no end play. Install the lock washer, then the outer nut, and torque the outer nut to 150 ft-lb. Pulling this preload too tight is the #1 cause of premature bearing failure on rebuilt Dana 44 hubs.

Pad slap (pulling old pads, throwing in new ones, ignoring rotor condition) is not a job on this truck. Measure the rotor with a vernier caliper; if it's at or below 0.96" thick, replace it. Resurfacing rusty Dana 44 rotors usually pulls them past discard.
steps: Loosen the lug nuts a half turn while the truck is on the ground. Jack the front, set stands under the frame rails.
Pull the wheels. Take a photo of the caliper, pin layout, and hose orientation before you start so reassembly is unambiguous.

Unbolt the caliper from the knuckle. On 1987–1992 trucks, use a hammer and a punch on the tension pins; on 1994–1996, remove the two slider bolts. Suspend the caliper from the coil/spring with a bungee.
Slide the old pads out of the bracket. Inspect bracket clips — replace if rusted.
Pry off the dust cap on the front of the hub. Bend back the lock tab on the lock washer. Loosen the outer locknut and lock washer, then the inner spindle nut.
Pull the hub/rotor assembly off the spindle. Catch the outer bearing as it falls out. Don't drop it.

Mount the new rotor onto a clean hub (or transfer the hub onto the new rotor if you bought rotor-only). Repack inner and outer bearings with high-temp wheel-bearing grease. Pack the cavity in the hub about half full of grease.
Slide the assembly back onto the spindle. Install the outer bearing, washer, then the inner spindle nut. Torque the inner nut to 50 ft-lb while rotating the rotor, then back off 45 degrees.
Install lock washer and outer nut. Torque outer nut to 150 ft-lb. Bend the lock washer tab onto the outer nut.

Compress the caliper piston with a C-clamp (with an old pad on the piston face). Slide new pads into the bracket. Mount the caliper. Torque caliper bolts to 30–45 ft-lb per Ford service spec (year-dependent).
Reinstall the wheel. Torque lugs to 100 ft-lb in a star pattern.
Pump the brake pedal until it's firm before moving the truck. Bed in the new pads with 6–8 moderate stops from 35 mph, then one or two harder stops from 50 mph (when traffic is clear).
pros: Restores braking distance immediately
Forces a wheel-bearing service that probably overdue anyway
Doable in a Saturday morning on jack stands
cons: Brake system; mistakes can kill someone
Year-specific caliper hardware — confirm tension-pin vs. two-bolt before buying
Bearing repack is messy and unforgiving of dirt in the bearings

title: Serpentine / V-Belt Service

parts.name: Gates K060915 serpentine belt — 5.0L/5.8L with A/C (91.5")
Gates K060790 belt — power steering bypass (79.0")

summary: A 1992–1996 5.0L or 5.8L Bronco with A/C runs a 91.5-inch serpentine belt (Gates K060915). Pre-1992 trucks have multiple V-belts, one per accessory. Either way, the belt is a $30 part that strands you on the side of the road when it lets go.
description:
The Full-Size Bronco's belt service depends on which generation you have. The 1992–1996 trucks (Gen 5) use a single serpentine belt with a spring-loaded automatic tensioner — the same setup most modern trucks use. The 1980–1991 trucks (Gen 3 and Gen 4) use multiple V-belts, one per pair of accessories, each adjusted with a slotted bracket. The 1978–1979 first-generation big Bronco also runs V-belts, but with different pulley sizes and a smaller-block engine option.

Replace the belt at 60,000 miles or sooner if you see glazing (a shiny surface from heat), cracks across the ribs, missing chunks from the ribs, or splitting along the edges. A squeal at startup or after a wet drive often means the belt is glazed and slipping on the alternator pulley. Don't bother with belt dressing — it masks the problem for a week, then the squeal comes back worse.

For the 5.0L and 5.8L Windsor with A/C and stock pulleys (the most common 1992–1996 configuration), the belt is a Gates K060915 — 91.5 inches, six-rib. If your truck has had a smog pump deleted, A/C deleted, or a different power steering pump, the belt length changes. The K060910 (91.0") fits some 5.8L configurations; the K060790 (79.0") works for a power-steering-bypass setup. Confirm the belt length by measuring the old one before ordering.

V-belt service on pre-1992 trucks is slower but uses cheaper belts. Each accessory has its own tension bracket. Loosen the bracket bolts, pivot the accessory toward the engine to slacken the belt, slide the belt off, install the new one, and pry the accessory outward to tension. The tension target is about 1/2-inch of deflection at the midpoint of the longest belt run. Too tight kills the accessory bearings (alternator, water pump, A/C compressor); too loose lets the belt squeal and slip.

There's a belt routing decal under the hood of most 1992–1996 trucks. If yours is faded, the LMR belt routing guide and forum threads cover every common configuration. Snap a photo of the old belt before removing it — that's the cheapest insurance.
steps: **1992–1996 serpentine:** Locate the automatic tensioner (driver-side, mid-engine, with a square 1/2-inch drive socket on the arm).
Put a 1/2-inch breaker bar or serpentine belt tool on the tensioner. Rotate the tensioner counterclockwise to slacken the belt.
Slip the belt off the easiest pulley to reach (usually the alternator). Release the tensioner slowly.
Compare the new belt to the old one — same length, same rib count. Route the new belt per the underhood decal or your reference photo. Save the crankshaft pulley for last.
Apply tension on the tensioner again, route the belt over the final pulley, slowly release.
Inspect the routing for misalignment. Run the engine for 30 seconds, check for noise or wobble.

**Pre-1992 V-belts:** Loosen the locking bolt and adjustment bolt on the accessory bracket. Pivot the accessory inward to release tension. Replace the belt. Pivot outward to tension — target 1/2-inch deflection at the longest run.
Tighten the locking bolt to spec (~30 ft-lb for most brackets). Recheck deflection. Run the engine, listen.
pros: $30 part, 30-minute job — easiest preventive maintenance there is
Catches a tensioner problem before the belt fails on the trail
Spare belt fits under the driver's seat for trail emergencies
cons: Wrong-length belt installs without complaint and then slips
The automatic tensioner itself wears out around 100,000 miles — if the new belt squeals, the tensioner is suspect, not the belt
V-belt era trucks (pre-1992) need each belt adjusted individually — over-tensioning kills accessories

title: Coolant Flush — 351W and 302

parts.name: Prestone DEX-COOL / All-Makes coolant concentrate, 1 gallon

summary: A 302 cooling system holds about 14 quarts. A 351W with auto trans and standard cooling holds 16 quarts (17 with super-cool or A/C). Run a 50/50 mix of concentrate and distilled water, and don't skip the block drains — they hold 4–5 quarts of old fluid even after the radiator is empty.
description:
The Windsor cooling system on a full-size Bronco is straightforward, but it has two traps that catch first-timers. Trap one: there are two block drain plugs (one on each side of the block, near the back), and if you don't open them the system stays half-dirty. Trap two: the heater core can hide air pockets that overheat the engine on the first hot afternoon after a flush. Backflushing the heater core during the flush is the difference between a clean job and an overheating cycle.

If the existing coolant looks brown, oily, or full of suspended brown flakes, this is a flush-and-fill job, not a drain-and-fill. The 351W in particular runs hot and the iron block sheds rust scale into old coolant. Pull a few ounces into a clear jar before you start — clear green or pink fluid means a basic drain-and-fill is enough; opaque brown means you need to flush with water two or three times before the new coolant goes in.

Use a 50/50 mix of coolant concentrate and distilled water. Tap water in Phoenix or anywhere with hard water leaves scale in the water jackets. The 50/50 ratio is the freeze/boil sweet spot — going richer than 60% concentrate actually reduces heat transfer.

The block drain plugs are 1/4" NPT brass and they sometimes round off when you turn them after 30 years untouched. Hit them with PB Blaster the night before and use a 6-point socket, not a 12-point. If one snaps, you can swap to a replacement plug from any hardware store NPT bin.

After refill, leave the radiator cap off, set the heater to max heat / max fan, and idle the engine until the upper hose gets hot. Top off as the air burps out of the thermostat housing. If the truck has the bleed screw at the thermostat housing (later 351W trucks), crack it until coolant streams out without bubbles.
steps: With the engine cold, remove the radiator cap. Position the drain pan under the radiator petcock (lower passenger side on most years).
Open the petcock and let the radiator drain. You'll get 4–6 quarts. Some petcocks are stiff; turn slow and don't break the tab.
Loosen the lower radiator hose at the radiator end if the petcock flow is weak — that will pull the rest of the radiator empty fast.
Move the drain pan under the driver's-side block drain. Crack the 1/4 NPT plug. About 2 quarts will come out. Repeat on the passenger side.
Disconnect the heater hoses at the firewall. Stick a garden hose into the inlet side and flush the heater core backwards until water runs clear out the outlet side. This is the step most people skip.
Reinstall block drains, lower hose, and heater hoses. Close the radiator petcock.
Fill with distilled water through the radiator. Run the engine to operating temp with the heater on full hot, then drain again. If the water comes out dirty, repeat the water flush.
Drain everything one final time. Fill with concentrate first (about half the system capacity), then top with distilled water.
Run the engine with the cap off, heater on, until the upper hose is hot and the level in the radiator stops dropping. Burp any air. Install the cap.
Check the level after a hot/cold cycle the next morning. Add coolant to the overflow bottle to bring it to "FULL COLD."
pros: Restores cooling capacity on a clogged system
Catches a marginal water pump or heater core before it lets you down on a trail
Routine done every 30,000 miles outlasts the engine
cons: Block drain plugs sometimes snap and need to be replaced
Heater core backflush is the step everyone skips
Used coolant is a regulated waste — needs proper disposal

title: Differential Fluid — Dana 44 Front, Ford 9-Inch Rear

parts.name: Gear oil — 80W-90 GL-5 (1 quart x 5 needed)
Synthetic 75W-140 gear oil — for trail/towing rigs
Rear diff cover with drain plug (optional upgrade)

citations.title: Full-Size Bronco — Rear and front diff fluid

summary: The Dana 44 TTB front takes about 3.5–4.0 pints of 80W-90 GL-5 gear oil. The Ford 9-inch rear takes about 5.5 pints (a touch over 2.5 quarts). Add Motorcraft XL-3 friction modifier if the rear has a Trac-Lok limited slip — otherwise the clutches will chatter on tight turns.
description:
The Dana 44 TTB and Ford 9-inch are tough axles, but they aren't immortal. Trail use, deep water crossings, and 35,000-mile service intervals all push moisture and metal into the diff fluid. If your truck just came out of a creek, change the diff fluid before storing it overnight — water in the fluid emulsifies to a milky sludge and corrodes the bearings while the truck sits.

The front axle (Dana 44 TTB) has a fill plug only — no drain plug from the factory. To change it, you suck the old fluid out through the fill hole with a fluid pump, then refill. About 3.5–4.0 pints is the target. If the old fluid is gray, milky, or smells burned, you'll want to pull the differential cover (if your axle has one — TTBs don't all) or back off the carrier and inspect.

The rear axle (Ford 9-inch) is the bigger procedure. The 9-inch is a third-member design — meaning the gear set unbolts as a unit from the front of the housing. For a fluid change, you don't pull the third member; you remove the rear cover instead. That gives you a chance to inspect ring-and-pinion contact pattern, scrape the magnet, and re-seal. Some 9-inch housings don't have a removable cover (the integral-housing earlier trucks) — those require pulling the third member to drain. Check what you have before you start.

For Trac-Lok limited slips, the friction modifier is not optional. Skip it and the clutches will chatter — you'll hear a banging or popping noise from the rear axle in low-speed turns. The modifier is a 4-ounce bottle that goes in with the fresh gear oil.

Synthetic 75W-140 is worth the upgrade if you tow, run 35"+ tires, or do any sustained low-range work. The extra film strength is real, and 75W-140 holds up to heat soak better than conventional 80W-90 in slow trail miles. For a daily-driver Bronco in Phoenix that sees pavement and dirt roads, conventional 80W-90 is fine.
steps: Run the truck for 10 minutes to warm the fluid — warm fluid drains faster and pulls more contamination out with it.
Park on level ground. Set the parking brake. Chock the wheels.

**Front axle:** Wipe the area around the fill plug clean. Crack the fill plug *first* — if it won't come out, stop before you drain anything. Pump the old fluid out with a hand pump into a catch pan. Pump fresh 80W-90 in until it dribbles out the fill hole. Reinstall the fill plug, torque to 25 ft-lb.

**Rear axle (cover-style):** Slide a 5-gallon drain pan under the diff. Loosen the bottom row of cover bolts first, leaving the top two finger-tight. Crack the bottom of the cover with a pry bar to start the drain.
Once the flow slows to a trickle, remove the remaining cover bolts and pull the cover. Catch the magnet — if it's a beard of metal slivers, the diff has problems beyond a fluid change.
Scrape the old gasket/RTV off both mating surfaces with a plastic scraper. Clean both surfaces with brake cleaner.
Apply a continuous 1/8" bead of anaerobic RTV to the cover, going inside the bolt holes. Bolt the cover on within 5 minutes. Snug the bolts in a star pattern to 25–30 ft-lb.
Let the RTV cure for an hour before adding fluid. Fill through the diff fill hole on the cover (some aftermarket covers have a top fill plug instead) until fluid runs out — that's the level.
If Trac-Lok rear, add 4 oz of Motorcraft XL-3 friction modifier before the gear oil reaches the fill level.
Reinstall fill plug, torque to 25 ft-lb. Wipe down the housing, drive a few miles, check for seepage at the cover.
pros: Cheapest insurance against bearing failure in the field
Forces inspection of the magnet — early warning on gear/bearing trouble
90-minute job per axle for a fluid change
cons: Front-axle service is suck-and-fill if your axle has no drain plug — fluid pump needed
9-inch housings without a removable cover require pulling the third member
Trac-Lok chatter from skipping the friction modifier sounds like (and gets misdiagnosed as) failing U-joints

title: Oil Change — 5.0L and 5.8L Windsor V8

parts.name: Motor oil — 6 quarts 10W-30 conventional (early trucks, hot climates)

citations.title: Ford Bronco Oil Type — All Model Years (Jim Burke Ford)

summary: Both the 5.0L and 5.8L Windsor V8 take 6 quarts of motor oil with a fresh FL-1A filter. Use 5W-30 in 1989–1996 trucks and either 5W-30 or 10W-30 in 1978–1988 trucks — pick the heavier grade if you live somewhere hot and the engine has miles on it.
description:
The Windsor V8 in any full-size Bronco was designed around the FL-1A filter and a 6-quart sump. Ford updated the recommended viscosity to 5W-30 across the entire model range in a later TSB, so even on a 1980 truck running 5W-30 is acceptable. In Phoenix or anywhere else that bakes the engine bay, 10W-30 holds film strength better at temperature if your engine is past 150,000 miles or runs a touch loose. Don't overfill — putting 7 quarts in because someone told you "another quart for the filter" foams the oil and pushes it out the rear main.

The drain plug is at the rear of the pan, takes a 15/16" socket on most years, and uses a soft aluminum or copper crush washer that should be replaced every other change. The oil filter screws onto a boss on the driver's side of the block. On TTB trucks (1980–1996), the filter sits behind the front axle beam — you'll catch oil on the beam and on the front driveshaft if you yank the filter without a long-spout funnel or a finger dam under it. A piece of cardboard between the filter and the axle saves cleanup.

Hand-tighten the new filter after wiping the mating surface and pre-oiling the gasket. Three-quarter turn past contact is enough; do not use a filter wrench to install. Torque the drain plug to 20–25 ft-lb on the rear sump bolt — these aluminum-washer plugs strip aggressively if you go to 40.

Run the engine for a minute, check for leaks at the filter and drain plug, then shut it down and recheck the dipstick after five minutes. Stop adding oil when the level is at the upper mark, not above it.
steps: Warm the engine for 2–3 minutes so the oil flows out fully, then shut it off.
Raise the front of the truck on the frame rails and set jack stands. Wheels can stay on the ground if you have decent ground clearance.
Slide the catch pan under the rear of the oil pan. Crack the drain plug with a 15/16" socket, then back it out by hand and let it drop into the pan as the oil starts to flow.
While it drains, position the catch pan under the filter, then unscrew the filter counterclockwise. Brace for a half-cup of oil running down your forearm.
Wipe the filter mounting surface clean. Pre-oil the new filter's rubber gasket and hand-spin it on until the gasket contacts the block, then go three-quarter turn past contact.
Install the drain plug with a fresh crush washer. Torque to 20–25 ft-lb.
Pour in 6 quarts of motor oil through the valve cover fill cap.
Start the engine and watch the oil pressure gauge come up within 2–3 seconds. Look under the truck for leaks. Shut down, wait five minutes, and verify the dipstick reads at the upper mark.
pros: Cheapest single piece of maintenance you can do
Catches metal in the filter media before it scores bearings
30-minute job once you have done it twice
cons: The filter location dumps oil on the front axle beam if you are sloppy
Aluminum drain-plug washers strip if you over-torque
Used oil pickup requires hauling the jug to a parts store or transfer station

title: Spark Plugs and Wires — 5.0 / 5.8L

citations.title: Full-Size Bronco — Spark plug torque thread

summary: Run Motorcraft SP-413 or Autolite 25 plugs gapped to 0.044" on the 5.0/5.8L Windsor. Torque to 15 ft-lb. Replace the wires at the same interval — old wires waste new plugs.
description:
The Windsor V8 in every full-size Bronco uses a tapered-seat plug with no gasket. Stock gap from the factory is 0.044". Don't deviate unless you've switched ignition systems — running a 0.054" gap on a stock TFI coil burns out the cap and rotor faster than it gains you anything. Motorcraft SP-413 (platinum, ~25,000-mile interval) is the conservative choice. Autolite 25 (copper, ~15,000-mile interval) is the cheap, predictable, proven option that has been in millions of these engines.

Wires are where most people leave money on the table. A worn set of wires arcs to the valve covers under load and the engine stumbles, surges, or pings under wide-open throttle. If the wires have brittle boots, cracked insulation, or any green-blue corrosion at the boot end, replace the set when you do plugs. Motorcraft factory wires are fine for daily use; MSD or Taylor 8.5–9mm aftermarket wires are worth the upcharge if you wheel in deep water or thread an extension hose for high-water crossings.

The driver's-side rear plug (cylinder 7) is the one that costs you knuckle skin every time. The exhaust manifold and the firewall are both right there. Use a 5/8" spark-plug socket with a rubber retainer, an extension, and patience. Anti-seize is optional on Motorcraft plugs — the threads come plated — but on Autolites, a single dab of nickel anti-seize on the threads is good insurance. Never anti-seize the electrode end.

Pull and replace one wire at a time so you don't cross firing order (1-3-7-2-6-5-4-8 on the 302 and 351W). Run a little dielectric grease inside each boot. Crank the engine for two seconds with the coil wire disconnected before reconnecting to clear any oil that fell down the plug well — this is a 351W habit that prevents the first start from misfiring.
steps: Let the engine cool fully. Hot exhaust on the driver's side will burn forearms.
Pull one plug wire by the boot, not the wire. If it sticks, twist a quarter turn first.
Blow compressed air or shop air around the plug base to push grit out of the well.
Loosen the plug with a 5/8" spark plug socket on an extension. Back it out by hand once it breaks loose.
Check the gap on the new plug with a gauge — aim for 0.044". Adjust the side electrode if needed.
Hand-thread the new plug fully before putting a wrench on it. Aluminum cylinder heads are unforgiving of cross-threading; cast-iron Windsor heads are forgiving but bad habits stay habits.
Torque to 15 ft-lb (or 1/16 turn past finger-tight if no torque wrench is handy).
Slide a dab of dielectric grease into the new boot, push the wire on until it clicks, and move to the next cylinder.
pros: Restores cold-start crispness on any tired 5.0/5.8
Fixes ignition misfires that look like fuel-system problems
Sub-$100 job that buys 25,000 miles of clean running
cons: Driver's-side rear plug is a knuckle-buster
Wires age faster than plugs in a hot engine bay
Cross-threading a plug in a cast-iron head still costs a Helicoil

title: Transfer Case Fluid — BW1356 / NP208

parts.name: Motorcraft XL-12 transfer case fluid (1 qt x 3)
Mercon V ATF — for NP208 only (do NOT use in BW1356)

summary: The BW1356 (1988–1996) takes Motorcraft XL-12, not regular ATF. The earlier NP208 (1980–1987) takes Mercon ATF. Putting gear oil in either case kills the internal pump. Capacity is roughly 3 quarts for the BW1356 and a hair over 3 quarts for the NP208.
description:
The transfer case is the part of the drivetrain people forget. It sits under the truck, takes abuse from rocks and creek crossings, and quietly grinds itself into shavings if the fluid never gets changed. Ford recommends 30,000-mile intervals. For a trail rig that sees water crossings, cut that to 15,000 miles or change after every deep-water trip.

Two transfer cases live under a Full-Size Bronco. From 1980 to 1987, you got the NP208 — a chain-driven, aluminum-housed case that uses Mercon ATF. From 1988 to 1996, Ford switched to the BW1356 (also called BorgWarner 1356) — also chain-driven, with an internal fluid pump for bearing lubrication. The pump is the reason fluid choice matters: it's designed to move ATF-viscosity fluid, and thick gear oil will starve the bearings.

There's a wrinkle on the BW1356. The original fluid spec was "Mercon ATF" — a Ford spec that has been discontinued for years. Mercon V replaced it for transmissions, but Mercon V contains a friction modifier that's wrong for transfer cases. Ford's current answer is Motorcraft XL-12, a dedicated transfer case fluid. Use XL-12 in the BW1356, or use a Mercon-replacement fluid specifically rated for transfer cases (AMSOIL Synthetic Transfer Case Fluid is the common upgrade). Don't use straight Mercon V.

For the NP208, plain Mercon ATF (or modern Mercon V) is fine. The NP208 doesn't have the same fluid-pump sensitivity.

If the fluid you drain is metallic, milky-white, or smells like burned electronics, the case has bigger problems than a fluid change can fix. Pull the magnet, inspect for steel chips, and budget for a rebuild or used replacement.
steps: Run the truck for 5–10 minutes to warm the fluid. Park on level ground.

Wipe the area around the fill plug at the upper-rear of the case. Crack the fill plug *first*. The plugs use a 3/8" square drive (a 3/8" ratchet handle fits directly into the plug — no socket needed). If the fill plug won't come out, stop. Don't drain a case you can't refill.
Position the drain pan. Remove the drain plug at the bottom-rear of the case. Let it drain for 10–15 minutes — the chain holds fluid.
Inspect the drain plug for chips and shavings. A light film of metal paste is normal at 30,000 miles. Visible chips or chunks of steel mean internal wear.
Clean both plugs. Reinstall the drain plug, torque to 20–25 ft-lb.

Refill through the fill hole using a hand pump. For the BW1356, use Motorcraft XL-12 (or equivalent Mercon-replacement transfer case fluid). For the NP208, use Mercon V ATF. Capacity is about 3 quarts; stop when fluid runs out the fill hole — that's the level.
Reinstall the fill plug, torque to 20–25 ft-lb. Wipe down the case, drive a few miles, recheck for seepage at the plugs and the rear-output seal.
pros: $25–60 in fluid avoids a $1,500+ transfer case rebuild
Drain plug inspection is the earliest warning sign of internal wear
A 60-minute job, no special tools beyond a 3/8" drive
cons: Wrong fluid in the BW1356 destroys the internal pump
Mercon V is *not* a drop-in for original Mercon spec in the BW1356 — get XL-12 or a verified transfer case fluid
Drain plug can be torqued in by a previous owner — keep a breaker bar handy

title: Radius Arm Bushing Replacement
tools_required: ball joint press or large vise

parts.name: Energy Suspension radius arm bushing kit (polyurethane)
Radius arm nut + retaining washer kit

citations.title: Radius arm bushing rubber or polyurethane (Full Size Bronco)

summary: Worn radius arm bushings let the front axle wander fore and aft under acceleration and braking — you'll feel it as a clunk on throttle-off or vague steering at highway speed. Energy Suspension 4.7110R is the standard polyurethane kit; rubber Moog bushings work for daily drivers that want a softer ride.
description:
The Full-Size Bronco's TTB front axle locates each beam fore-and-aft with a long radius arm running back to a frame mount. The radius arm bolts to the beam at the front and threads through a rubber bushing at the rear frame mount. That rear bushing takes every acceleration and braking force the front axle generates — the entire chassis pulls against it under acceleration, and the truck's mass pushes against it under braking. Rubber bushings collapse, crack, and eventually delaminate. The first symptom is a clunk when you transition between gas and brake.

Replacing the bushings tightens up the front end dramatically. A 25-year-old truck with original rubber bushings feels like the front axle is mounted to the frame by spaghetti. New bushings make it feel like a different vehicle.

Two material choices: polyurethane and rubber. Polyurethane (Energy Suspension 4.7110R) lasts substantially longer than rubber, transmits more road noise and vibration to the cabin, and locates the axle more rigidly under load. Rubber (Moog or OEM equivalent) rides softer and is quieter, but wears faster and lets more axle movement through. For a daily driver Bronco that sees pavement, rubber is fine. For a trail truck or a truck running larger tires, polyurethane is the better fit.

The color of the polyurethane (red vs. black) is purely aesthetic. Energy Suspension catalogs both. Pick whichever you like; the durometer (hardness) is identical.

The job itself is straightforward in concept and miserable in execution if the bushings have been in place for 25 years. The retaining nut at the rear of the radius arm is tight, exposed to road salt and grit, and torqued to 220+ ft-lb from the factory. Plan for a breaker bar, an impact gun, or a torch.

Lubricate polyurethane bushings on install with the included grease (silicone-based — *do not* use petroleum-based grease on polyurethane, it eats the material). Re-grease every 50,000 miles if you start hearing a squeak from the front end.
steps: Park on level ground. Chock the rear wheels. Loosen the front lug nuts a half-turn. Jack the front, support on stands under the frame rails. Front wheels off.

Find the radius arm rear mount (under the frame, behind the front axle, the long arm ends at a vertical mount with a big nut). Spray the nut and the threads liberally with PB Blaster. Let it soak for 15+ minutes.
Loosen the front coil spring tension by either removing the spring (lift trucks: pull spring; stock trucks: leave compressed) or jacking the beam to neutralize spring load on the radius arm.

Remove the radius arm rear retaining nut. This is the hard part — a 1-1/8" socket on a long breaker bar usually wins; an impact gun is faster. Some trucks need heat from a propane torch on the nut to break the rust bond.

Pull the rear washer, the rear bushing, the metal sleeve, and the front bushing off the rear stud as you remove the arm. Note the order — the front bushing sits against the frame mount, then the metal sleeve, then the radius arm threads through, then the rear bushing, then the washer and nut.
Clean the rear stud of the radius arm with a wire wheel. Inspect for cracking or thread damage.

Apply the polyurethane grease to the new bushings (both sides of each). Slide the front bushing into the frame mount, the metal sleeve through, the radius arm onto the sleeve, the rear bushing onto the stud, the washer, then the new nut.
Torque the rear nut to 220–250 ft-lb. This is a Class A fastener — use a torque wrench, not feel.
Drop the truck. Drive 50 miles and recheck the nut torque.
pros: Cures front-end clunk on acceleration/deceleration almost completely
Polyurethane lasts essentially the life of the truck
$45–90 part, 2–4 hour job — high return on investment
cons: Rear retaining nut is one of the most stubborn fasteners on the truck — budget for heat or an impact
Polyurethane transmits more NVH (noise, vibration, harshness) into the cabin
Wrong grease (petroleum-based) on polyurethane destroys the bushing in months — use only the silicone grease that comes with the kit
Misaligned bushings will squeak; if you get a squeak after install, the bushings are dry — re-grease, don't ignore

title: TTB Alignment After a Lift

parts.name: TTB pivot drop brackets — for 4"+ lifts

citations.title: TTB Lifted Wheel Alignment (Full Size Bronco)

summary: Lifting a TTB pushes camber positive (the top of the wheel tilts outward) and pulls caster low (the wheel wants to flop, not return to center). Adjustable caster/camber bushings handle up to about 2.5–4° of correction. Anything beyond a 4-inch lift needs pivot drop brackets to keep the geometry honest. Target spec on a lifted truck: 0° camber and +4° to +6° caster.
description:
The Twin Traction Beam axle is a geometry trap. Each beam pivots at the opposite frame rail, so when you lift the truck, the wheel swings on a long arc. That arc rotates the knuckle outward at the top (positive camber) and reduces the angle of the steering axis behind vertical (lowered caster). The truck will track straight if you ignore it, but the tires will scrub the outside shoulders to nothing in 8,000 miles, and the steering will refuse to self-center after a turn — you have to wrestle it back to straight.

The factory caster/camber range on a stock 1980–1996 Bronco is roughly: camber 0° to +1°, caster +2° to +4°. A 2.5-inch lift might push camber to +2° and caster down to +1° — borderline drivable, but the tires will wear funny. A 4-inch lift can push camber to +3° to +4° and caster down to 0° or even negative — undrivable on the highway without correction.

Three correction options, in increasing order of cost and lift height:

**Adjustable caster/camber bushings.** These replace the press-in upper ball joint sleeve with an eccentric (off-center) bushing. Rotating the bushing tilts the knuckle relative to the beam, which changes camber and caster. Common ratings are 1.5°, 2.5°, and 4° of adjustment. James Duff (dufftuff.com) makes 1.5° bushings; multiple vendors offer 2.5°. The 4° versions exist but the eccentric is so off-center that the ball joint life shortens.

**Alignment cams.** Eccentric cams that replace the upper ball joint sleeve fasteners. Same idea, different mounting style. Slightly easier to fine-tune than the bushing-style — you turn the cam, lock it down. About 2.5° of total range.

**Pivot drop brackets.** For 4-inch and taller lifts. These move the beam pivot points lower on the frame, which un-rotates the beam arc and brings camber/caster back toward stock geometry without changing the ball joint sleeves. They are the right answer for any lift over 4 inches but require drilling new mounting points in the frame or using new brackets — more involved than a bushing swap.

Target spec on a lifted Bronco: camber as close to 0° as possible (slightly negative is fine), caster +4° to +6°. Toe should be zero or slightly toe-in (1/16" total). Drive the truck for a week before declaring the alignment settled — TTB beams take some miles to relax into their final position after parts swaps.
steps: Drive the truck onto level ground, wheels straight. Bounce the front end (push down hard on the bumper, let it spring up — do this 3–4 times) to settle the suspension.
Measure current camber with a magnetic camber gauge on the rotor face (with the wheel off). Note the reading per side.

Measure caster: turn the wheels 20° one direction, read the camber gauge; turn 20° the other direction, read again. Caster is the difference between the two readings, divided by 2/3 (this is the "20-degree sweep" method).
For bushing-style adjustment: pop the upper ball joint pinch bolt at the top of the knuckle. Pry the knuckle slightly to release the upper ball joint sleeve. Unscrew the old sleeve.
Install the new adjustable bushing per its degree rating. Orient the high side of the eccentric to correct camber outward (toward the engine) and caster rearward.
Torque the new sleeve to its spec (varies by brand; James Duff calls for 40 ft-lb on the sleeve, then 100–110 ft-lb on the pinch nut).
Drop the truck, re-measure. Adjust bushing orientation as needed. Goal: 0° camber, +4° to +6° caster per side.

Set toe last. With the wheels straight, measure the distance between the front edges of the tires and the rear edges of the tires (at hub height). Front edge should be 1/16" closer than the rear (slight toe-in). Adjust by loosening the tie rod adjuster sleeve clamps and rotating the tie rod.
Drive 50–100 miles and recheck. If alignment shifted, the ball joint sleeve seated further; re-do the camber/caster pass.
pros: Brings a lifted truck back to highway-stable steering and even tire wear
Caster correction kills steering wander and brings self-centering back
DIY-able if you have a magnetic camber gauge and patience
cons: Adjustable bushings are extreme on 4"+ lifts — pivot drops are the better answer there
TTB geometry is not perfectly correctable; you're approximating, not solving
The factory alignment shop may refuse to align a lifted TTB beyond their specs sheet — find a 4x4 specialty shop in advance
A 6"+ lift on TTB is fundamentally a poor geometry choice; solid axle swap (SAS) starts to make more sense at that height

title: TTB Dana 44 Service (1980-1996)

citations.title: Dana 44 & Dana 44HD TTB Front Axles (Blue Oval Trucks)
Ball Joint Tech and Questions (Full Size Bronco)

summary: The TTB Dana 44 is two independent beam halves pivoting at the frame, with ball joints, wheel bearings, axle seals, and a locking hub at each end. Service is a multi-stage teardown — plan for a weekend, not an afternoon. Moog K8195T (lower) and K80026 (upper) are the long-running standard ball joints.
description:
The Twin Traction Beam Dana 44 is Ford's compromise axle: solid-axle articulation on the trail, IFS-style ride comfort on pavement. Each "beam" is a half-axle that pivots at the opposite side of the frame, so the wheels can move independently like an IFS but the axle shaft and ring gear sit at solid-axle height. The trade-off is geometry: lifting a TTB changes camber dramatically because the beam swings on a long arc.

Service items on the TTB Dana 44 break down into four categories, listed in order of likely failure:

**Ball joints.** Two per side. Lower carries the cornering load and wears out first — usually between 80,000 and 150,000 miles. The first sign is a clunk when transitioning from acceleration to braking, or wandering steering. Moog K8195T (lower) and K80026 (upper) are the standard parts. Don't buy budget ball joints for a vehicle this heavy.

**Wheel bearings.** Tapered roller bearings with a thrust washer and spindle nut. They use a "set the preload by feel" procedure — tighten the nut while spinning the rotor, back off, retighten to spec, then back off 1/6 turn. A loose preload feels like a wobble in the steering wheel at highway speed. An over-tight preload destroys the bearings in 500 miles.

**Inner axle shaft seal.** The seal where the inner stub passes through the differential housing. When it fails, gear oil pumps out into the inner axle tube and contaminates the wheel bearings. Smell the wheel bearing grease — if it smells like gear oil, the inner seal is gone.

**Locking hubs.** Manual locking hubs (Warn Premium, Mile Marker) are standard on most 1980–1989 trucks. 1990–1996 trucks got automatic hubs from the factory, which are widely hated for unreliable engagement. Most owners swap auto hubs to manuals (Warn Premium being the gold standard) within the first year of ownership.

Ball joint torque sequence matters. The factory pattern is: lower nut to 70–90 ft-lb, upper sleeve to 40 ft-lb, upper nut to 100–110 ft-lb. After install, check "pull torque" by hooking a fish scale to the steering arm — 12 to 26 lb at the scale is the in-spec range. Below 12 means the joints are loose; above 26 means binding (which will eat the joints in months).

D44 ball joints and D50 ball joints are *not* interchangeable, despite looking similar. Confirm you have a Dana 44 (smaller knuckle, smaller-diameter shafts) before ordering parts.
steps: Set the parking brake, chock the rear wheels. Loosen the front wheel lug nuts a half-turn each. Jack the front, support on stands under the frame. Remove the wheels.
Pop the locking hub cover. Remove the snap ring and the hub assembly. Inspect for missing/stripped teeth.
Bend the lock tab on the outer spindle nut, remove the outer nut, the lock washer, then the inner spindle nut. The hub/rotor assembly slides off.
Pull the spindle bolts (six total). Tap the spindle with a brass hammer to break it free. Slide the spindle and stub axle out.
Remove the tie rod end (separator tool) from the steering knuckle.

To service ball joints: support the beam, remove the brake caliper and rotor, then the upper ball joint pinch bolt at the top of the knuckle. Unscrew the upper joint sleeve. Press the lower joint out with a ball joint press (rented from auto parts stores).

Install new joints: press the lower in first. Torque to 70–90 ft-lb. Install the upper sleeve to 40 ft-lb, then the upper nut to 100–110 ft-lb. Verify pull torque at the steering arm with a fish scale: 12–26 lb is in spec.

Reinstall in reverse: stub axle (with fresh inner seal if doing seals), spindle (torque bolts to 50 ft-lb), spindle nut to spec (snug while spinning, back off, snug to ~50 ft-lb, back off 1/6 turn, install lock washer + outer nut to 60 ft-lb).
Reinstall locking hub (rebuilt or new). Greased, with the snap ring and cover seated correctly.
Reinstall tie rod end, torque to 60 ft-lb, install fresh cotter pin.
Wheel back on, lower the truck. Alignment is required — the camber/caster will have shifted with the ball joint work.
pros: Combines wheel bearing, ball joint, seal, and hub service into one teardown
Moog ball joints will go another 100,000 miles if the geometry is right
Manual locking hubs from this service onward are dramatically more reliable than the OEM auto hubs
cons: This is a full weekend job for a first-timer — set aside time
Ball joint pull torque is not a guess: under-torque and they're loose, over-torque and they bind
Lifted trucks need adjustable alignment bushings to get camber back in spec — see TTB alignment guide
Alignment shop after the work is non-negotiable; the steering geometry resets entirely
